detailedSolution:
**Quick Answer:** Karl Marx identified Alienation as the defining condition of workers in a capitalist factory.

**Concept:**
In capitalist manufacturing, workers do not own the tools or the goods they produce, transforming creative labor into repetitive, deskilled, alienated wage labour.

**Step-by-Step Breakdown:**
Marx identified four dimensions of alienation under industrial capitalism:
1. Alienation from the product: The worker does not own or control what is made.
2. Alienation from the work process: Work is coerced, monotonous, and controlled by machines.
3. Alienation from fellow workers: Workers are forced into wage competition.
4. Alienation from human nature (species-essence): Creative potential is reduced to a commodity.

The Green Revolution was largely funded by international agencies. It

inequalities. In most of the Green Revolution areas, it was primarily the
medium and large farmers who were able to benefit from the new

marginal farmers could not afford to spend as much as large farmers to
purchase these inputs. When agriculturists produce primarily for
themselves and are unable to produce for the market, it is known as
‘subsistence agriculture’ and they are usually termed ‘peasants’.

and above the needs of the family, and so are linked to the market. In many
cases, the Green Revolution led to the displacement of tenant-cultivators.

directly because cultivation was becoming more profitable. This made the
rich farmers better off, and worsened the condition of the landless and
marginal holders.

The Green Revolution was largely funded by international agencies. It
focused on providing high-yielding variety (HYV) or hybrid seeds along
with pesticides, fertilisers, and other inputs, to farmers. Green Revolution
programmes were introduced only in areas that had assured irrigation,
because sufficient water was necessary for the new seeds and methods of
cultivation. It was also targeted mainly at the wheat and rice-growing areas.
As a result, only certain regions such as the Punjab, western U.P., coastal
Andhra Pradesh, and parts of Tamil Nadu were targeted. Though, it
managed to increase the agricultural output, it also resulted in increased
inequalities. In most of the Green Revolution areas, it was primarily the
medium and large farmers who were able to benefit from the new
technology. This was because inputs were expensive, and small and
marginal farmers could not afford to spend as much as large farmers to
purchase these inputs. When agriculturists produce primarily for
themselves and are unable to produce for the market, it is known as
‘subsistence agriculture’ and they are usually termed ‘peasants’.
Agriculturists or farmers are those who are able to produce surplus, over
and above the needs of the family, and so are linked to the market. In many
cases, the Green Revolution led to the displacement of tenant-cultivators.
For landowners began to take back land from their tenants and cultivate it
directly because cultivation was becoming more profitable. This made the
rich farmers better off, and worsened the condition of the landless and
marginal holders.
